item.title: Dissertation Chapter 2 — The Development of Consumption Theory: A Review of the Literature
item.description:
Chapter 2 The Development of Consumption Theory: A Review of the Literature

Compared with growth and growth theory, consumption was for a long time not the most important field of theoretical research in macroeconomics, because the sufficiency of consumption itself — which is closely connected with man’s natural needs — seemed, relative to the utilisation of scarce resources, to be self-evident. For this reason, in the classical economics that began with Adam Smith, consumption was only a variable lying far beyond productive capacity: how to satisfy “it” was the ultimate goal of economic theory, and even the comparatively well-developed theory of demand did not connect consumption with macroeconomic development. Only after Keynes (John Maynard Keynes) had constructed modern macroeconomics was this situation thoroughly reversed. The modern macroeconomics founded by Keynes not only opened up the research paradigm of analysing macroeconomic aggregates; against the background of the capitalist crisis of relative overproduction it also paid greater attention to the analysis of demand. From the time we entered the Keynesian era, demand and consumption became important links driving the healthy operation of the economy. Still more important was the introduction of the “consumption function”, and the series of policy practices conducted around “effective demand” achieved good results; from this point, research on consumption formally entered the field of systematic economic research. The policy practices conducted under the guidance of Keynesian theory placed government purchases, monetary policy, investment activity and the like all around demand, so that in this sense Keynesian economics is in fact an economics of demand management. Although demand includes more than consumption, from this moment consumption did indeed combine with demand to become an important field of research in modern macroeconomics. Looking at the process of development of consumption theory, on the one hand it developed as real productive forces gradually developed, material products gradually became abundant, the role played by the market in economic activity gradually grew stronger, and mankind gradually developed from “shortage” to the stage of “relative overproduction”; on the other hand it also developed as economic thought gradually evolved and improved, and research objectives, methods and angles gradually became richer.

item.title: Dissertation Chapter 3 — The Formation and Development of the Cash-Flow Consumption Model
item.description:
Chapter 3 The Formation and Development of the Cash-Flow Consumption Model

The economy is a complex composite in which universal connections exist among its factors; problems in the sphere of consumption therefore cannot be connected with the sphere of consumption alone, nor can the solution to consumption problems be sought only at the link of consumption itself. It is necessary to analyse comprehensively income, finance, money, financial markets, the age structure of the population, years of work, the social security system, and every other aspect. It may be said that consumption is the final link in the whole cycle of society’s material production, and that the various contradictions in the sphere of consumption are in large part the concentrated expression of contradictions at the links of production and circulation. The primary reason for insufficient consumption demand, for example, may be that income is low, which in turn leads to insufficient consumption demand; or income may increase year by year while unfair income distribution leads to structural insufficiency of consumption demand. It is not necessarily the case that continually growing household saving alongside persistently sluggish consumption means that the return on saving is higher than the return on other investment; it is more likely that an increase in households’ expected risk has raised the precautionary motive; and the dependence of households’ consumption model for large consumer goods on saving rather than on income and future income is not necessarily caused by consumption habits, but is rather a rational decision made in pessimistic expectation of future employment, income, and social security.

item.title: Dissertation Chapter 4 — The Continuation of the Cash-Flow Consumption Model in the Early Stage of Marketization Reform
item.description:
Chapter 4 The Continuation of the Cash-Flow Consumption Model in the Early Stage of Marketization Reform

Under the planned economic system there were profound institutional reasons why residents’ consumption displayed a “cash-flow model” and a “dependence on saving”, but these institutional reasons began to loosen after 1978. As the economic system made its transition from plan to market, the economic behaviour of enterprises, of the government, and of households began to be marketized. In this period the residents’ consumption rate grew considerably, but the cash consumption model underwent no fundamental change: the behavioural characteristics of depending on saving, and of depressing everyday consumption in order to reach a saving target, persisted. The marketization reform of this stage therefore did not touch the sphere of consumption and consumers; it was merely a quantitative effect brought about by the increase in the economic aggregate and the quickening of its growth — that is, the increase in the aggregate did not change the conditions constraining consumers’ behaviour, so that the consumption model neither could nor needed to change, and it was on precisely this basis that the original consumption model was continued.

item.title: Dissertation Chapter 5 — The Foundations and Paths of the Transformation of the Consumption Model
item.description:
Chapter 5 The Foundations and Paths of the Transformation of the Consumption Model

The profound changes produced by the acceleration and deepening of China’s construction of a market economy are manifested not only in the various economic indicators, but have gradually also come to be manifested in the behaviour of the government, of enterprises, and of consumers. At the same time, because the process of transition of China’s economic system has been relatively rapid, various forms of maladaptation have accompanied the marked performance in economic efficiency. On the government side, the shift from the past comprehensive management of the economy to the present position, in which the economy can be regulated only through fiscal and monetary policy and a part of administrative power, has left the government, when macroeconomic regulation is needed, with scant means and insufficient experience; in a crisis, a government lacking experience of market management may therefore make wrong decisions, and thereby, in the process of the market as a multi-player game, exert a negative influence on economic efficiency and equity alike. On the enterprise side, marketization has brought enterprises freedom, but has at the same time imposed on their survival the hard constraint of profit. Enterprises, as economic units whose ultimate goal is the pursuit and realisation of efficiency, no longer bear, as the “work units” of the past did, an excessive obligation of “equity”, and this has made the mode of enterprise management approach more closely that of the “economic man”. The disappearance of the various implicit welfare benefits formerly paid by the “work unit” has accordingly had a very great influence on workers’ incomes, and bears on the raising of workers’ utility and welfare; this missing part of welfare is the greatest crux of China’s present market economy reform. Finally, the employment environment, the mode of income, the social security system, and so on faced by all consumers have likewise undergone substantive change, and these changes in the constraint conditions have caused consumption behaviour to change. None of these changes is isolated; they are profoundly connected with one another and possess corresponding logical links. To discuss the transformation of the consumption model, one must therefore discuss every aspect connected with the consumer and its logical links, including the distribution of labour income, the perfection of capital and financial markets, the perfection of the social security system, and the present-day problem of household housing.

item.title: Dissertation Chapter 6 — The Risks and Obstacles in Developing the Balance-Sheet Consumption Model
item.description:
Chapter 6 The Risks and Obstacles in Developing the Balance-Sheet Consumption Model

As the economy develops and people’s living standards rise, and as the content of consumer goods grows richer and their quality improves, the transformation of the consumption model is in fact a process that occurs naturally as the market economy and free competition gradually deepen — especially once assets and large consumer goods have gradually become the principal objects of consumption. Yet this process of transformation, which ought to “occur naturally”, often fails to take shape because of various risks and obstacles. Since China is to establish a sound operating mechanism and environment for a market economy, realising the transformation of the consumption model in accordance with the laws of the market economy is the road that must be travelled; removing the various obstacles that impede the transformation of the consumption model and reducing the risks of the transformation thus become major problems that must be solved in setting out on this road. It has been demonstrated above that, under the cash-flow consumption model, consumption displays unstable volatility and consumers’ utility improves only slowly, and that these restrict the potential of economic development from both the supply side and the demand side. The balance-sheet consumption model is a correction of, and an evolution from, the cash-flow model; but having resolved the old contradictions it gives rise to new problems — namely, that matters such as the cash flow, asset returns and bankruptcy risk that an enterprise faces in its operations become important elements in consumers’ safe operation and even in macroeconomic security and stability. Analysing the types, magnitudes and movements of the risks internal to the balance-sheet consumption model is therefore a necessary condition for demonstrating that the transformation of the consumption model can succeed; and analysing the actual state of existence of these conditions is at the same time an important step in removing the obstacles to the transformation of the consumption model.

item.title: Dissertation Chapter 7 — International Experience and Policies for Launching Consumption
item.description:
Chapter 7 International Experience of the Transformation of Consumption Models and Policies for Launching Consumption

Under the market economy model, the contribution of China’s household consumption to economic growth has long been lower than that of the investment and trade sectors, and, compared with other countries, the contribution of consumption to the economy also lags considerably. Although, as a matter of theoretical logic, we cannot simply deduce what level of consumption rate is appropriate, or which country’s consumption model is the reasonable one, by comparing the differing economic foundations, consumption models, consumption policies and consumption-related policies of various countries we can still arrive at an orientation for the consumption model relatively suited to the next stage of China’s development. In addition, analysing and comparing the consumption models of different countries at different points in time can provide an appropriate starting point and frame of reference for China’s strategy for the transformation of its consumption model.

item.title: The Transformation of Consumption Patterns in China's Marketization Process
item.description:
Jian Mu · PhD dissertation, School of Economics, Renmin University of China, 2011 · Supervisor: Professor Zhenhua Mao

Why did China’s household consumption rate keep falling through the fastest growth decades in its history — and what would it take to turn consumption into the engine of growth? This dissertation builds a cash-flow / balance-sheet model of household consumption across China’s marketization: from the planned-economy consumption model, through its continuation in early reform, to the foundations, risks, and international lessons of the transformation still under way.

item.title: China's Low Consumption Rate and Stage-Based Household Expenditure
item.description:
Jian Mu

School of Economics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872

Originally published in Chinese in Lanzhou Academic Journal, 2010, No. 3, pp. 50–54. Translated from the author’s manuscript.

Abstract: Building on life-cycle theory, permanent income theory, and the theory of precautionary saving, and taking into account China’s deep-rooted family values, this paper puts forward the concepts of stage-based expenditure and the intergenerational expenditure cycle. On the basis of these two concepts, it analyses the income and expenditure behaviour of Chinese households and the relationships among asset prices, income, and the consumption rate, and offers, from a new perspective, an explanation of China’s problem of under-consumption and directions for reform.

item.title: Building China's Social Welfare System During Economic Adjustment
item.description:
Jian Mu

School of Economics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872

Originally published in Chinese in Theory Horizon (Lilun Jie), 2009, No. 12, pp. 6–8. Translated from the author’s manuscript.

Abstract: A financial crisis originating in the United States is profoundly affecting China’s economy. For the world, this is the second great economic recession since 1929; but for China, this financial crisis, which has already spread to it, is the first cyclical adjustment it has faced under marketization. China has established a socialist market economy system, but the building of the related welfare system remains incomplete. Against this background, China will face risks different from those of the past; these risks will affect future economic development and the improvement of welfare levels. Avoiding these risks will ultimately depend on appropriate economic instruments and on the building of democratic institutions.

item.title: Restructuring the Regional Development Model
item.description:
Jian Mu

Originally published in Chinese in Journal of Hexi University, 2005, Vol. 21, No. 4, pp. 14–17.

Abstract: By summarising regional development models and, at the same time, drawing on a new classification of resources and on the concept of macro differential rent, this article reconstructs the framework of regional development models, incorporating the old models into the new framework so that they stand alongside the original models without contradiction. Within the new analytical framework, it also analyses each specific region with its own characteristics, so that in reality a specific region can more easily find the development model suited to itself.
